answer:
# NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Password Length Requirements (answers to the three asks)

Source of truth: NIST SP 800-63B-4, *Digital Identity Guidelines, Authentication and Authenticator Management*, July 2025 (final revision). Normative language is from Sec. 3.1.1 (Passwords), the numbered requirements list, items 1 and 2. Corroborating sources carrying identical text: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/ , the final PDF https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=959882 (NIST SP 800-63B-4, July 2025), and the single-page view https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html .

## Verbatim normative text

> "Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length. Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length."
>
> "Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters."

Supporting text from the same section (relevant to how the numbers are counted and bounded):

> "Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD accept Unicode [ISO/ISC 10646] characters in passwords. Each Unicode code point SHALL be counted as a single character when evaluating password length."
>
> "Verifiers MAY make limited allowances for mistyping (e.g., removing leading and trailing whitespace characters before verification, allowing the verification of passwords with differing cases for the leading character) if the password remains at least the required minimum length after such processing and the complexity of the resulting password is not significantly reduced."

And from the usability guidance (Sec. 3.1.1 usability considerations), consistent with the maximum:

> "Allow at least 64 characters in length to support the use of passphrases."

## Answers

1. **Single-factor password minimum: 15 characters.** SP 800-63B-4 Sec. 3.1.1: "Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length." This is a SHALL — a hard requirement on verifiers and CSPs.

2. **Password used only as part of multi-factor authentication: minimum 8 characters.** Same section: "Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length." The shorter 8-character floor applies only when the password is not used as a stand-alone single-factor authenticator; when it is the sole factor, the 15-character minimum applies.

3. **Maximum: verifiers SHOULD permit at least 64 characters.** Same section: "Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters." This is a floor on the maximum — i.e., a compliant verifier should allow passwords up to at least 64 characters (a SHOULD-level recommendation, not a SHALL). It is consistent with the informative Appendix A (Strength of Passwords) guidance to "Allow at least 64 characters in length to support the use of passphrases."

## Enforcement notes for implementers

- Count length in Unicode code points, not bytes or grapheme clusters ("Each Unicode code point SHALL be counted as a single character when evaluating password length").
- After any permitted mistype normalization (e.g., trimming leading/trailing whitespace), the password must still satisfy the applicable minimum (15 or 8).
- Do not impose composition rules, do not require periodic changes, do not store hints, and do not use KBA/security questions at password selection; verify the full submitted password without truncation (same section, items 5–9).
- Minimum length summary table for policy configuration:
  | Password usage | Minimum length (SHALL) |
  |---|---|
  | Single-factor authentication mechanism | 15 characters |
  | Component of multi-factor authentication only | 8 characters |
  | Maximum length permitted (SHOULD, floor) | at least 64 characters |

## Notes on versioning and on the harness proofs of absence

- The December 2022 initial public draft (NIST.SP.800-63B-4.ipd.pdf) used the term "memorized secrets" and required "at least 8 characters" with a "SHOULD permit at least 64" maximum, without the 15-character single-factor tier. That draft is superseded by the July 2025 final SP 800-63B-4, which is the revision named in the request; the figures above are the final revision's.
- The grounding contains harness-made proofs of absence for asks 2 and 3 against one page only: https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=957668 , which is NIST SP 800-63Bsup1, *Incorporating Syncable Authenticators* (April 2024) — a supplement about syncable authenticators and key cloning, 19 pages. The harness searched that full text and found none of "8 characters", "at least 8 characters", "minimum of 8 characters", "characters" (ask 2) and none of "64 characters", "at least 64 characters", "maximum of 64 characters", "64", "characters" (ask 3). Those proofs are scoped to that supplement page and no other. That supplement is not the source of the password-length rules and is not the document the request asks about; SP 800-63B-4 itself states both figures verbatim on the pages cited above. Accordingly the answers to asks 2 and 3 are not "the page states none": the values 8 and 64 characters are stated by SP 800-63B-4, so no ask is placed in not_stated and no figure is withheld.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 3.1 on pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators and 5.1 on nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-63b-4.ipd.pdf. The first reads: "3.1.4.1), except they require the presentation and verification of an activation factor (i.e., a password or a biometric characteristic) to obtain the OTP from the authenticator."
